title: Construction of taurine metabolism-related risk model and subtype identification in colorectal cancer to predict prognosis and immunological features

sections.abstract:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a significant global health burden. Despite advances in treatment, survival rates remain low for patients diagnosed at advanced stages. Although taurine plays an indispensable role in cancer development and progression, its specific relationship with CRC prognosis has not been fully explored. Therefore, this study aims to construct a prognostic model based on taurine metabolism-related genes (TMRGs) to evaluate its potential value in CRC risk stratification, tumor microenvironment remodeling, and the development of personalized treatment strategies.

This study integrated multi-omics data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) databases to systematically screen differentially expressed TMRGs (DETMRGs). Using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and multivariate Cox analysis, we constructed a prognostic model and established a risk stratification framework. Molecular subtyping was performed based on these signature genes, followed by a comprehensive evaluation of the immune microenvironment (CIBERSORT/ESTIMATE), tumor mutational burden, drug sensitivity (pRRophetic/CellMiner), and immunotherapy response [immunophenoscore (IPS)/IMvigor210 cohort] to thoroughly validate the clinical predictive utility of the model.

This study identified 175 DETMRGs and constructed a prognostic model comprising 9 key genes. The model demonstrated robust survival predictive capability in both training and independent validation cohorts [area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) >0.74], effectively stratifying patients into molecular subtypes with significant survival disparities. In-depth analyses revealed that the high-risk group was enriched in pro-oncogenic signaling pathways (e.g., WNT, RTK-Ras) and exhibited an immunosuppressive microenvironment (elevated Treg infiltration, reduced immune scores) with inferior response to programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. Conversely, the low-risk group activated immune-related pathways (e.g., JAK-STAT) and showed heightened sensitivity to chemotherapy agents such as 5-fluorouracil (5-FU).

The taurine metabolism-related risk model developed in this study reliably predicts the prognosis of CRC patients and their response to immunotherapy, thereby enabling personalized treatment strategies.

Keywords: Colorectal cancer (CRC), taurine metabolism, prognostic model, subtypes, immune response
sections.introduction:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cause of cancer globally and the second most common cause of cancer-related mortality ( 1 ). It is a heterogeneous malignant disease originating from the epithelial cells of the colorectal mucosa and represents one of the major malignant tumors worldwide with high incidence and mortality rates ( 2 ). The development and progression of CRC involve a complex multi-step process, including epigenetic alterations, aberrant signaling pathways (such as Wnt/β-catenin, p53, and KRAS), and dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment ( 3 - 5 ). Its incidence is also closely linked to environmental and lifestyle factors, where a high-fat/low-fiber diet, obesity, and smoking increase the risk of developing the disease ( 1 , 6 ). The incidence of CRC is higher in men than in women ( 7 , 8 ), and significant geographic disparities exist in both its incidence and mortality rates globally. The highest rates are observed in affluent Western countries, while the lowest rates are found in low-income countries (such as those in Africa or South Asia) ( 9 ). Recent research has unveiled a novel mechanism in which the long non-coding RNA HOTTIP drives CRC progression by regulating the Hedgehog signaling pathway and promoting HUWE1-mediated degradation of the p53 protein ( 10 ). Despite advancements in surgical techniques and chemotherapy regimens, the overall survival (OS) rate remains low, particularly for patients diagnosed at advanced stages. This underscores the urgent need for novel biomarkers and more effective systemic therapies to improve outcomes for patients with this challenging malignancy.

Taurine, a sulfur-containing β-amino acid, is widely distributed in mammalian tissues and organs, with particularly high concentrations in the heart, brain, and skeletal muscle ( 11 , 12 ). It serves as a crucial organic osmolyte in the human body, exhibiting multiple physiological functions including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, ion balance regulation, and cell membrane protection ( 13 - 16 ). In recent years, its role in cancer has garnered increasing attention. Intratumoral administration of high-dose taurine enhances mitochondrial fitness in CD8⁺ T cells, significantly improving the efficacy of anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy ( 17 ). Taurine remodels the tumor immune microenvironment by modulating ROS levels and PD-1 expression, thereby determining whether lung cancer undergoes immune escape or immune activation, and consequently either promoting or suppressing cancer progression ( 18 ). A previous study demonstrated that taurine is significantly associated with increased odds of CRC, with elevated expression levels observed in CRC patients—particularly when measured in blood-based matrices ( 19 ). However, the relationship between taurine metabolism and CRC prognosis remains unclear. Understanding this association may facilitate the development of novel metabolism-based cancer therapeutics.

To elucidate the prognostic and immunological significance of taurine metabolism in CRC, we integrated transcriptomic profiles from multiple cohorts and systematically identified taurine metabolism-related signature genes. Through rigorous bioinformatics modeling, we constructed a novel risk stratification system and defined molecular subtypes. This integrated approach establishes a framework for evaluating the clinical impact of taurine metabolism while providing insights into tumor microenvironment heterogeneity and potential therapeutic vulnerabilities in CRC. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD reporting checklist (available at https://jgo.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/jgo-2025-638/rc ).
sections.methods:
RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data for colon adenocarcinoma [The Cancer Genome Atlas-Colon Adenocarcinoma (TCGA-COAD): 41 normal, 473 tumor] and rectal adenocarcinoma [TCGA-Rectal Adenocarcinoma (READ): 10 normal, 167 tumor] were acquired from UCSC Xena database ( https://xena.ucsc.edu/ ). These cohorts were merged to create a combined CRC training set (51 normal, 640 tumor). Synchronously, the latest copy number variation (CNV) profiles and corresponding clinical annotations were retrieved from TCGA portal ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). Patients without survival records were excluded. For validation, two microarray datasets ( GSE29623 : n=155 tumors; GSE103479 : n=65 tumors) were obtained from Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ). Additionally, 610 taurine metabolism-associated genes were curated from MSigDB database ( https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb ). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments.

Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified by performing differential expression analysis between the CRC tumor group and the normal group using the “limma” package (thresholds: |log fold change (FC)| >1, adj.P.Val <0.05). Resultant DEGs were intersected with taurine metabolism-related genes (TMRGs), identifying 175 differentially expressed TMRGs (DETMRGs). These underwent Gene Ontology (GO)/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis using “clusterProfiler”. Following clinical data integration and exclusion of cases with survival <30 days, univariate Cox regression (“survival” package; P<0.05) identified prognostic DETMRGs, whose chromosomal locations were mapped using “RCircos”.

Prognostic DETMRGs (P<0.05) from univariate analysis were used to construct the model, with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression (“glmnet” package) employing cross-validated λ-selection to eliminate correlated genes and prevent overfitting. Subsequent multivariate Cox regression (“survival” package) established the final model, enabling risk score calculation via signature gene expression and coefficients. Patients were stratified into high/low-risk groups using median scores, where survival curves and timeROC-generated area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) (1-/3-/5-year) evaluated predictive accuracy alongside visualizations of risk distributions, survival status plots, and signature gene Kaplan-Meier curves. Validation confirmed robustness through replicated survival/ROC analyses, consistent risk stratification, and individual gene prognostic assessment.

Consensus clustering of CRC samples was performed using the “ConsensusClusterPlus” package based on the identified signature genes. Survival analysis across subtypes was conducted via the “survival” package. DEGs between subtypes were identified with thresholds of |logFC| >0.585 and adj.P.Val <0.05, followed by GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses using “clusterProfiler”.

The CRC samples underwent consensus clustering analysis through the “ConsensusClusterPlus” package, utilizing the identified signature genes for classification. Subsequent survival analysis comparing different molecular subtypes was performed using the “survival” package. Differential gene expression analysis between subtypes was carried out with stringent criteria (absolute logFC >0.585 and adjusted P value <0.05), followed by comprehensive functional annotation through GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses implemented in the “clusterProfiler” package.

GSEA v4.3.2 was conducted to identify enriched pathways between high- and low-risk groups. Meanwhile, differential expression analysis was performed across risk groups. Subsequent GO and KEGG signaling pathway enrichment analyses of the resulting DEGs were executed using the “clusterProfiler” R package.

Integrating clinical parameters with risk scores, combined Cox regression analyses constructed a nomogram (“rms” package) predicting 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival, with calibration curves validating accuracy and prognostic independence, followed by decision curve analysis (DCA) (“ggDCA” package).

Immune infiltration scores for cell types and functional signatures were quantified via single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) across subtypes/risk groups, while the estimate package computed Immune, Stromal, ESTIMATE Scores, and Tumor Purity. CIBERSORT further resolved infiltration disparities. Immune checkpoint gene expression was comparatively analyzed across stratifications. Immunophenoscore (IPS) and TIDE scores for TCGA-COAD/READ cohorts were sourced from TCIA ( https://tcia.at ) and TIDE ( http://tide.dfci.harvard.edu/ ) portals, respectively, with comparative analyses evaluating risk-group differentials. Based on previous research, a dataset of patients with bladder urothelial carcinoma who received anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (anti-PD-L1) therapy was collected from the IMvigor210 cohort, and the samples were stratified into high- and low-risk groups using the constructed model ( 20 ).

Mutation profiles from TCGA-COAD and TCGA-READ cohorts were analyzed to compute per-sample tumor mutation burden (TMB), with GenVisR visualizing mutational patterns of the top 20 mutated genes across risk groups.

Candidate drugs demonstrating significant sensitivity-signature gene expression correlations were screened via CellMiner database ( https://discover.nci.nih.gov/cellminer/ ), while the pRRophetic package predicted therapeutic compound Half Maximal Inhibitory Concentration (IC50) values in high-/low-risk subgroups.

Statistical analyses were conducted in R software (v4.4.0), with group comparisons performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Correlation analyses examined variable relationships through both Pearson and Spearman approaches, with statistical significance established at P<0.05.
sections.results:
Based on clustering analysis of TCGA-COAD and TCGA-READ samples, both cancer cohorts were merged ( Figure 1A ). Differential analysis between tumor and normal groups identified 3,667 DEGs, comprising 1,770 upregulated and 1,897 downregulated genes ( Figure 1B ). Intersection of these DEGs with TMRGs yielded 175 DETMRGs ( Figure 1C ). GO enrichment analysis of these genes reveals significant enrichment in categories such as transmembrane transporter activity for carboxylic acid, lipids, and organic acids, as well as the cell basal part. KEGG enrichment analysis shows that these genes are mainly involved in pathways like neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, bile secretion, taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, and drug metabolism ( Figure 1D,1E ). Univariate Cox regression analysis of DETMRGs identified 21 prognostic genes (P<0.05) ( Table S1 , Figure 1F ). Notably, only six genes ( GCG , CRYAB , ELANE , MS4A1 , XDH , and LEP ) exhibited lower expression in tumor tissues compared to normal samples, while all others showed upregulated expression in tumors. Inter-gene correlation patterns and chromosomal positions were visualized through heatmap and genomic mapping analyses ( Figure 1G-1I ).

DETMRGs identification and functional analysis. (A) PCA plot of training set sample distribution. (B) Volcano plot of DEGs between tumor and normal groups. (C) Intersection analysis of DEGs and TMRGs. (D) GO enrichment analysis of DETMRGs. (E) KEGG enrichment analysis of DETMRGs. (F) Forest plot of univariate analysis for prognostic genes. (G) Box plot of prognostic gene expression. (H) Heatmap of prognostic gene co-expression patterns. (I) Circos plot of prognostic gene genomic locations. *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001. BP, biological process; CC, cellular component; CI, confidence interval; COAD, colon adenocarcinoma; CRC, colorectal cancer; DEGs, differentially expressed genes; DETMRG, differentially expressed TMRGs; Dim, dimension; FC, fold change; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genome; MF, molecular function; PCA, principal component analysis; READ, rectal adenocarcinoma; TMRG, taurine metabolism-related gene; TMRGs, taurine metabolism-related genes.

LASSO regression on 21 candidate genes yielded 15 signature genes ( Table S2 ; Figure 2A,2B ), refined to 9 prognostic genes via multivariate Cox regression ( Table S3 ; Figure 2C ). Risk scores calculated for clinical samples showed training cohort AUCs of 0.781 (1-year), 0.747 (3-year), and 0.739 (5-year) ( Figure 2D ), with Kaplan-Meier analysis confirming significantly reduced OS in high-risk patients ( Figure 2E ). Risk distribution and survival status plots validated prognostic utility ( Figure 2F ). Validation cohorts ( GSE29623 / GSE103479 ) maintained AUCs >0.75 across timepoints with consistent high-risk mortality trends ( Figure 2G,2H ). Expression analysis revealed significant upregulation of GABRD, LEP, TIMP1, TERT and PHGDH in high-risk versus low-risk groups ( Figure 2I ), while GABRD, TIMP1, OVGP1, TERT, PHGDH, GABRB1 and KPNA2 were elevated in tumors ( Figure 2J ). All signature genes exhibited significant survival associations in expression-stratified Kaplan-Meier curves ( Figure S1 ).

Prognostic model development and validation. (A) LASSO coefficient trajectories. (B) Cross-validation for optimal λ. (C) Multivariate Cox selection of 9 signature genes. (D) Training cohort ROC curves (1/3/5-year). (E) Kaplan-Meier survival curves. (F) Risk/survival distributions (training). Validation cohorts: (G) GSE29623 and (H) GSE103479 ROC/Kaplan-Meier/risk distributions. (I) Risk-group gene expression. (J) Tumor-normal differential expression. *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001. AIC, Akaike information criterion; AUC, area under the ROC curve; CI, confidence interval; LASSO, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator; ROC, receiver operating characteristic.

Consensus clustering of CRC tumor samples was performed using the “ConsensusClusterPlus” package based on signature genes, with optimal cluster determination at K=2, where the consensus matrix demonstrated clear segregation into two distinct blocks ( Figure 3A-3C ). PCA analysis confirmed robust subtype classification ( Figure 3D ), with survival analysis revealing significantly poorer outcomes in group 2 ( Figure 3E ). Enrichment analysis of inter-subtype DEGs identified immune-related processes, including granulocyte/leukocyte migration, chemotaxis, humoral immune response, and antibacterial humoral response ( Figure 3F ); KEGG pathway analysis showed significant enrichment in immune-inflammatory pathways (cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, chemokine signaling, IL-17 signaling pathway) ( Figure 3G ). Signature gene expression profiling indicated significantly elevated ELANE, TIMP1, and LEP in group 2 ( Figure 3H ). Comprehensive immune characterization revealed: (I) CIBERSORT analysis showing increased infiltration of B cells naive, plasma cells, T cells CD4 memory resting and mast cells activated in group 1 ( Figure 3I ); (II) ssGSEA indicating globally reduced immune cell populations and functional activity in group 1 ( Figure 3J ); and (III) ESTIMATE algorithm quantifying significantly lower immune/stromal/ESTIMATE scores but higher tumor purity in group 1 versus group 2 ( Figure 3K ).

Molecular subtyping of CRC based on prognosis-related DETMRGs. (A) Consensus clustering heatmap based on prognosis-related DETMRGs. (B) CDF plot for cluster stability. (C) Relative change in area under CDF curve. (D) Inter-subtype clustering analysis. (E) Kaplan-Meier survival curves for different molecular subtypes. GO (F) and KEGG (G) enrichment analysis of inter-subtype DEGs. (H) The expression of the 9 signature genes in group 1 and group 2. (I) CIBERSORT box plot of different subtypes. (J) ssGSEA immune infiltration in different subtypes. (K) ESTIMATE analysis of tumor microenvironment components. Group 1 and group 2 are two subtypes classified based on consensus clustering. ns, not significant; *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001. CCR, C-C chemokine receptor; CDF, cumulative distribution function; CRC, colorectal cancer; DEG, differentially expressed gene; DETMRG, differentially expressed taurine metabolism related genes; GO, Gene Ontology; HLA, human leukocyte antigen; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes; PC, principal component; ssGSEA, single-sample gene set enrichment analysis.

GSEA revealed high-risk enrichment in RTK-Ras-ERK signaling pathway, RTK-Ras-PI3K signaling pathway, FAK-CDC42 signaling pathway, and WNT signaling pathway; while the low-risk group included cytokine JAK-STAT signaling pathway, EGF-EGFR actin signaling pathway, homologous recombination, and tight junction actin signaling pathway ( Figure 4A,4B ). The GO enrichment analysis about DEGs highlights significant categories such as extracellular matrix (ECM) organization and collagen fibril organization, while the KEGG enrichment analysis emphasizes pathways like cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and cytoskeleton in muscle cells ( Figure 4C,4D ).

Enrichment analysis in risk groups. GSEA results of high- (A) and low-risk (B) groups. GO (C) and KEGG (D) enrichment of DEGs between high- and low-risk group. DEG, differentially expressed gene; GO, Gene Ontology; GSEA, gene set enrichment analysis; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes.

Evaluation of the CRC risk model through univariate assessment revealed significant associations between survival outcomes and multiple variables, including the risk Score, age, stage, and tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) stage ( Figure 5A ). Multivariate regression analysis demonstrated that survival outcomes remained significantly associated only with the risk score, age, stage, and M stage ( Figure 5B ). A nomogram incorporating clinical parameters was developed to predict patient survival probability ( Figure 5C ). DCA demonstrated robust predictive performance of the nomogram for 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival probabilities ( Figure 5D ). In addition, calibration curves were presented to assess the performance of the nomograms, which showed that the predicted curves of the model are close to the ideal ones ( Figure 5E ). Statistical analysis of clinical characteristics (age, gender, and TNM stage) revealed significant differences in risk score between M0 vs. M1, N0 vs. N1–2, T1+2 vs. T3+4, stage I + II vs. stage III + IV ( Figure S2A ). Kaplan-Meier analyses stratified by age (≤65 vs. >65 years), gender (female vs. male), stage (stage I + II + III vs. stage IV), T stage (T1+2 vs. T3+4), N stage (N0 vs. N1–2), and M stage (M0 vs. M1) consistently demonstrated reduced OS in the high-risk subgroups ( Figure S2B ). Additionally, in the training set, the 1-, 3-, and 5-year ROC curves of the nomogram and its individual components were compared, and the results demonstrated that the nomogram overall has excellent predictive performance ( Figure S3 ).

Establishment and assessment of the nomogram survival model. (A) Univariate Cox regression for the clinicopathologic characteristics and the risk score. (B) Multivariate analysis for the clinicopathologic characteristics and the risk score. (C) A nomogram was established to predict the prognosis of CRC. (D) DCA for predicting 1-, 3- and 5-year survival. (E) Calibration plots for 1-, 3- and 5-year survival rates. CI, confidence interval; CRC, colorectal cancer; DCA, decision curve analysis; f, full model; M, metastasis; N, node; T, tumor.

The ssGSEA algorithm showed that compared to the low-risk group, the high-risk group exhibited significantly higher levels of Treg, macrophages, plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), and T helper cells, as well as higher immune function scores ( Figure 6A ). ESTIMATE analysis revealed that high-risk group exhibited significantly higher Immune Score, Stromal Score, and ESTIMATE Score, whereas low-risk group demonstrated elevated tumor purity ( Figure 6B ). CIBERSORT analysis further indicated that high-risk group had significantly higher infiltration of T cells regulatory (Tregs), NK cells activated, macrophages M0, and mast cells resting, while low-risk group displayed elevated infiltration of plasma cells, T cells CD4 memory resting, dendritic cells activated and eosinophils ( Figure 6C ). Analysis of immune checkpoint gene expression revealed significant differences between the high- and low-risk groups ( Figure 6D ). IPS scores revealed that the low-risk group had significantly higher IPS scores than the high-risk group ( Figure 6E ). The response to PD-L1 blockade immunotherapy was analyzed in the IMvigor210 cohort. In this cohort, survival analysis revealed significantly better outcomes in the low-risk group compared to the high-risk group ( Figure 6F ). We categorized stable disease (SD) and progressive disease (PD) as non-response (NR), while complete response (CR) and partial response (PR) were classified as response (R). The results showed that the response rate was higher in the low-risk group than in the high-risk group ( Figure 6G ). Additionally, the risk score distribution was found to be lower in R patients compared to NR patients ( Figure 6H ). Then, a correlation heatmap was produced to illustrate the relationship between immune cell infiltration and signature gene expression ( Figure 6I ).

Immune microenvironment characterization. (A) ssGSEA immune cell (up) and immune function scores (down) for risk groups. (B) ESTIMATE analysis of tumor microenvironment components. (C) CIBERSORT immune cell fractions in high- and low-risk groups. (D) Differential immune checkpoint expression between high- and low-risk groups. (E) IPS score comparison between high- and low-risk groups. (F) Survival analysis of the IMvigor210 cohort in high- and low-risk groups. (G) Immunotherapy response rate comparison between high- and low-risk groups. (H) Risk score distribution plot between the immune response R group and NR group. (I) Correlation heatmap between signature genes and immune cell infiltration. ns, not significant; *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001. Corr, correlation; IPS, immunophenoscore; NR, no response; R, response; ssGSEA, single-sample gene set enrichment analysis.

Using TCGA mutation data, we calculated TMB in both the high- and low-risk groups. A waterfall plot of the top 20 genes with the highest mutation burden revealed that both groups exhibited high mutation rates in TP53, APC, TTN and KRAS ( Figure 7A ). Sensitivity to chemotherapy drugs was analyzed in patients. Results showed that the high-risk group had consistently higher IC50 values for 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), cetuximab, and lapatinib, whereas the low-risk group showed higher IC50 values for sorafenib ( Figure 7B ). Using the CellMiner database, we investigated the correlation between characteristic gene expression and drug sensitivity, revealing that TIMP1 exhibited a negative correlation (cor) with fluorouracil (cor =−0.267) and oxalipiatin (cor =−0.318), while TERT showed a positive correlation with fluorouracil (cor =0.276) and irinotecan (cor =0.425) ( Figure 7C , Table S4 ).

Tumor mutation and drug sensitivity analysis. (A) Waterfall plot of top 20 mutated genes in high- (up) and low- (down) risk groups. (B) Boxplots of drug sensitivity for 5-fluorouracil, sorafenib, cetuximab, and lapatinib in high- and low-risk groups. (C) CellMiner-derived drug-gene correlations. cor, correlation; IC50, half maximal inhibitory concentration.
sections.discussion:
This study explores the role of DETMRGs in CRC by integrating TCGA datasets. We developed a prognostic model using 9 key signature genes, which effectively stratified patients into high and low-risk groups, demonstrating significant survival differences. Molecular subtyping revealed distinct immune profiles and pathway enrichments, highlighting the impact of immune responses and inflammation on CRC progression. Our genomic and pharmacogenomic analyses identified mutation patterns and drug sensitivities, suggesting personalized treatment approaches. The findings emphasize the importance of taurine metabolism in CRC and provide valuable insights for future research and therapeutic strategies, potentially improving patient outcomes through tailored interventions.

These 9 key signature genes delineate the central role of taurine in CRC pathogenesis. In CRC, GABRD expression is significantly increased and associated with advanced pTNM stages and unfavorable patient survival. Overexpression of GABRD accelerates cell growth and migration, while its knockdown exerts inhibitory effects ( 21 ). The ELANE gene-encoded neutrophil elastase exerts selective cancer-killing effects in malignancies by releasing the CD95 death domain to bind histone H1 and induce cancer cell apoptosis, while simultaneously activating immune responses to suppress tumor growth and metastasis ( 22 , 23 ). TIMP1 has a dual role in cancer: on the one hand, it exerts tumor-suppressive effects by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) ( 24 ); on the other hand, it can support tumor progression by promoting cell proliferation, inhibiting apoptosis, and other mechanisms ( 25 ). KPNA2 functions as an oncogene in multiple cancers by facilitating nucleocytoplasmic transport of critical signaling molecules (e.g., transcription factors, oncoproteins), thereby promoting tumor proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and chemoresistance, with its overexpression significantly correlating with poor patient prognosis ( 26 , 27 ). In this study, elevated KPNA2 expression was similarly significantly associated with adverse prognosis. OVGP1 regulates ECM integrity and cell adhesion, thereby affecting tumor cell migration and metastasis ( 28 , 29 ). The leptin encoded by the LEP gene exerts oncogenic effects in various cancers, primarily through activating signaling pathways such as JAK/STAT and PI3K/AKT/mTOR to promote tumor cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( 30 ). TERT promoter mutations trigger telomerase activation, a key mechanism promoting tumorigenesis and advancement in multiple cancer types ( 31 ). Silencing PHGDH in primary tumors promotes cancer cell metastasis, as PHGDH interacts with PFKP to enhance cell migration and invasion ( 32 ). High expression of the GABRB1 gene in medulloblastoma is associated with better patient prognosis ( 33 ), in agreement with our findings demonstrating that elevated GABRB1 expression correlates with favorable outcomes. These genes play critical roles in tumors, with their expression levels significantly associated with patient prognosis.

The GO enrichment analysis of DEGs in CRC highlights significant categories such as ECM organization and collagen fibril organization, which are crucial for maintaining tissue structure and integrity ( 34 , 35 ). In cancer, remodeling of the ECM results in abnormal collagen fiber alignment, where collagen fibers in primary tumors become crimped and disorganized, while those in metastatic tissues display dense, linear, and directionally coherent arrangements ( 36 ). This abnormal arrangement is closely associated with tumor progression. Taurine inhibits the accumulation of ECM—a critical precursor to carcinogenesis—by eliminating activated hepatic stellate cells (primary ECM producers) through dual induction of ferroptosis and autophagy suppression, thereby disrupting the fibrotic microenvironment that drives hepatocellular carcinoma development ( 37 ). KEGG enrichment emphasizes pathways like cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and cytoskeleton in muscle cells, indicating roles in immune response modulation and cellular architecture ( 38 , 39 ). In CRC, cytokine receptor interactions activate STAT3 and NF-κB signaling pathways, thereby facilitating tumor invasion ( 40 ).

In this study, analysis of CRC immune microenvironment revealed significant disparities between high- and low-risk groups. The high-risk group exhibited increased infiltration of Tregs, macrophages, pDCs, and T helper cells, indicating a more pronounced immunosuppressive milieu that promotes tumor progression by suppressing effective anti-tumor immunity ( 41 , 42 ). This aligns with recent studies emphasizing the role of Tregs and macrophages in shaping an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment associated with poor prognosis across multiple cancers ( 43 , 44 ). This immunosuppressive microenvironment manifests as a lower IPS, indicating greater immune evasion potential. Consequently, in the IMvigor210 cohort, the high-risk group exhibited reduced response rates to PD-L1 blockade immunotherapy and poorer survival outcomes. Conversely, the low-risk group demonstrated higher tumor purity alongside elevated infiltration of plasma cells, resting CD4⁺ memory T cells, activated dendritic cells, and eosinophils, suggesting enhanced immune surveillance capabilities that inhibit tumor growth ( 45 ). Research indicates these immune populations contribute to robust anti-tumor responses, thereby improving patient survival rates.

Pharmacogenomic disparities among risk-stratified CRC patient cohorts reveal the profound impact of taurine metabolism on therapeutic efficacy: high-risk patients exhibit intrinsic resistance to 5-FU, cetuximab, and lapatinib, while low-risk tumors demonstrate sorafenib resistance due to preserved homologous recombination capacity. These findings underscore the critical importance of implementing risk stratification strategies in CRC treatment, wherein high-risk patients may require alternative therapies or combination approaches to overcome drug resistance, whereas low-risk patients can benefit from targeted or conventional chemotherapy.

This study highlights the potential of TMRGs in CRC prognosis and treatment stratification. However, this study has limitations. We primarily relied on OS data from the TCGA database, rather than disease-specific survival (DSS) data. For CRC, particularly for early-stage patients cured by surgery, long-term OS follow-up data are inevitably confounded by non-CRC-related mortality events, such as other comorbidities or deaths attributable to the “natural history” of aging. Consequently, the long-term predictive performance of our model may partially reflect patients’ overall health status rather than specifically capturing CRC progression. Future validation of this model’s predictive value for CRC-specific mortality requires multi-center, large-sample cohorts incorporating DSS data. Future research should focus on integrating multi-omics data, exploring taurine metabolism’s role in tumor immunity, and developing targeted therapies to enhance personalized treatment strategies for CRC patients.
sections.conclusion: This study successfully constructed a taurine metabolism-related risk model for CRC, which demonstrates predictive value for immunotherapy. It highlights the critical role of taurine metabolism in the progression of CRC and provides valuable insights for developing targeted therapies to improve patient outcomes.
